questions.heading: Best-First Solves the Fewest Nodes Because It Never Opens a Node Below the Optimum
questions.stem: A best-first search on a 0-1 model with 300 variables has 2 million nodes waiting and is about to run out of memory. Which change keeps the waiting list small?

options.text: Switch to depth-first, which leaves about one sibling behind per level
options.says: Right: each step down leaves one sibling waiting, so the list stays near the depth of the tree, at most about 300.

options.text: Switch to breadth-first, which clears each level before going deeper
options.says: Breadth-first keeps a whole level waiting, and levels double in size; it held the most nodes of all three rules.

options.text: Switch to breadth-first, and branch on the most fractional variable
options.says: Breadth-first keeps whole levels waiting whatever the variable rule: 2,839 at most with most-fractional, against 14 for depth-first.

options.text: Keep best-first, but branch on the first fractional variable instead
options.says: The variable rule changes the tree's shape, but best-first still returns to shallow nodes and leaves deep ones waiting.

questions.heading: The Variable Rule Decides Which Fractional Variable to Split
questions.stem: A node's LP sets x1 = 0.92, x2 = 0.58, x3 = 0.15 and x4 = 1.0. Which variable does the most-fractional rule branch on?

options.text: x1, since 0.92 is the largest of the values below 1
options.says: 0.92 is only 0.08 from 1; the rule wants the value farthest from both 0 and 1.

options.text: x4, since a value of exactly 1 is the most settled
options.says: A whole value is not fractional at all, so it is never a candidate for branching.

options.text: x2, since 0.58 is 0.42 from the nearer of 0 and 1
options.says: Right: the distances to the nearer whole number are 0.08, 0.42 and 0.15, and 0.42 is the largest.

options.text: x3, since 0.15 is the smallest of the nonzero values
options.says: 0.15 is 0.15 from 0; the rule takes the largest distance to the nearer whole number, not the smallest value.

questions.heading: Strong Branching Buys a Smaller Tree With Extra LPs
questions.stem: Strong branching tries two candidates at a node. Splitting x_a lowers the children's LP values by 30 and by 0.5; splitting x_b lowers them by 6 and by 5. Scored the way this lesson scores candidates, which one is chosen?

options.text: x_a, since one of its children drops furthest, by 30
options.says: One large drop with a tiny one leaves the second child almost as hard as the parent; the score multiplies both.

options.text: x_b, since both of its children drop by a good amount
options.says: Right: the product rewards a split that lowers the bound on both sides.

options.text: x_a, since its two drops add up to more than x_b's
options.says: The score is the product of the drops, not their sum; the sum would favour lopsided splits.

options.text: Either one, since both splits keep the same set of plans
options.says: Every split is correct, but the rule exists to pick the one that shrinks the tree, and the scores differ.
